# How `async` and `defer` work on `<script>`

## The baseline: an external classic script with neither attribute

An external classic script with neither attribute blocks the parser. The WHATWG HTML standard says: "If neither attribute is present, then the script is fetched and evaluated immediately, blocking parsing until these are both complete." (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html). web.dev adds that rendering is blocked as well as parsing (https://web.dev/learn/performance/optimize-resource-loading).

## `defer` on a classic external script

- **Parsing:** the script downloads in parallel with parsing and does not block it. It runs only after the document has finished parsing (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html).
- **Spec mechanism:** a parser-inserted deferred script is added to the document's "list of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing." The same list also holds module scripts.
- **DOMContentLoaded:** deferred scripts run after parsing and before DOMContentLoaded fires. They also hold the event back until they have run. MDN and web.dev both say this (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script, https://web.dev/articles/efficiently-load-third-party-javascript).
- **Caveat on the spec:** the spec's parsing section ("the end"), which defines this step, returned HTTP 404 to my researcher. So the timing relative to DOMContentLoaded is supported by MDN and web.dev, not by the spec text itself.
- **Order:** several deferred scripts run in the order they appear in the document (MDN; web.dev).

## `async` on a classic external script

- **Parsing:** the script downloads in parallel with parsing and runs as soon as it is available, "potentially before parsing completes" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html). If it finishes downloading while the parser is still working, running it interrupts DOM construction (https://web.dev/articles/efficiently-load-third-party-javascript).
- **Spec mechanism:** async scripts go into an unordered *set* of "scripts that will execute as soon as possible."
- **Order:** there is no ordering guarantee. MDN says "You get no guarantee that scripts will run in any specific order." web.dev says async scripts are likely to run out of document order.
- **DOMContentLoaded:** none of the sources ties async scripts to DOMContentLoaded. web.dev only guarantees that they run before the window's `load` event. My conclusion that an async script can run either before or after DOMContentLoaded is an inference from that missing guarantee, not a quoted statement.

## Both attributes on the same script

If both are present, `async` wins. MDN says the element acts as if only `async` were specified. The spec explains why you would write both: `defer` lets legacy browsers that support only `defer` fall back to deferring instead of blocking (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html).

One researcher, who was not allowed to open the spec, reported this fallback point as unsourced. Another researcher did open the spec and quoted it, so it is sourced.

## Inline classic scripts (no `src`)

`async` and `defer` have no effect on inline classic scripts. MDN warns against using either attribute there. Inline classic scripts run immediately and block the parser (MDN; https://web.dev/learn/performance/optimize-resource-loading).

## `type="module"` scripts

- **Deferred by default:** module scripts are deferred automatically, and web.dev says this applies to inline module scripts too. They do not block the parser (https://web.dev/learn/performance/optimize-resource-loading).
- **`defer` does nothing:** MDN says "The defer attribute has no effect on module scripts — they defer by default."
- **`async` does change behaviour:** with `async`, a module "and all their dependencies" are fetched in parallel to parsing and run as soon as they are available (MDN).
- **Inline modules don't run synchronously:** one researcher reported that the spec queues a task before running an inline module. They gave no quote for this, so I treat it as unverified.

## Gaps and disagreements

**Unconfirmed points.** I could not confirm these with any opened source:
- that `async` specifically works on *inline* module scripts;
- that a module included several times runs only once.

The javascript.info and v8.dev pages that were meant to cover these returned 404.

**Wording differences.**
- **web.dev's two pages:** https://web.dev/learn/performance/optimize-resource-loading says deferred scripts run "at the same time as" DOMContentLoaded. The other web.dev article and MDN's attribute reference say "before". "Before" is the more precise statement.
- **MDN's Examples section:** it says defer scripts "load" in page order, which means *execute*. It also says they run once "everything has finished loading", which conflicts with MDN's own attribute section. I relied on the attribute section.

**Script-inserted scripts.** web.dev notes that scripts injected into the DOM with JavaScript behave like async scripts.
